blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Define the division of labour, explain how it raises what each worker produces, and weigh its drawbacks for the worker as distinct from those for the employer and the wider economy.

blocks.heading: One task each
blocks.text: The division of labour, also called specialisation, splits production into separate narrow tasks so that each worker concentrates on one task instead of making the whole product. Namib Signs in Walvis Bay once built each signboard from design to fitting; after the split, one worker designs, one cuts metal, one paints, one fits - and the boards move from task to task along the workshop.

blocks.heading: Why output rises
blocks.text: Practice at one narrow task builds speed and skill; no time is lost moving between tools and stages; training a new worker for one task takes less time than teaching the whole craft; and each worker settles into the task that suits them. An assembly plant in Nagoya, Japan, grew on this pattern: a worker who spends the year tightening one set of bolts does it faster and with fewer faults than a craft worker who builds whole vehicles.

blocks.heading: What the worker gives up
blocks.text: Repeating one narrow task may bring boredom and low job satisfaction, and it ties the worker's livelihood to that single task: where the product changes or demand for it falls, the specialised worker's risk of losing work grows, because moving means learning a new task from the start. Drawbacks at the level of the whole economy - depending on a narrow range of production - belong to the economy, not to the person at the bench, and answers must keep the two apart.

blocks.heading: Whose benefit, whose drawback?
blocks.text: Asked how the division of labour benefits workers, some learners write that the firm's training costs fall - a benefit to the firm, not to the worker doing the task. Asked for a drawback to workers, some write about a country depending on a single export - a drawback to the economy. The test is to ask whose position the answer changes: the person at the bench, the business employing them, or the whole economy. Naming the party the question asks about is what earns the marks.

blocks.heading: For the firm and for the economy
blocks.text: The firm gains from the division of labour through higher output per worker and a lower average cost for each unit: the Namib Signs workshop makes more boards from the same wage bill, trains a new hand in days, and can buy machines suited to each narrow task. It also carries risks. Each stage depends on the one before it, so where the painter is off sick or the cutting machine breaks down, the whole line may stop. Repetitive work may breed boredom, which tends to raise absence, staff turnover and careless mistakes, and each of those adds to the firm's costs. For the economy, specialisation tends to raise total output, so more goods and services are available, often at lower prices, and regions and countries can trade what they produce best - Namibia exporting fish and minerals, for example, and importing machinery. The drawback for the economy is dependence: a town built around one specialised activity is exposed when demand for that product falls, and workers whose skills do not transfer may face long spells of unemployment.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: Specialisation changes what workers produce and so the supply examined in topic 2.4; the employers who divide the work, and their sectors, are the firms of topic 3.5; and the earnings of specialised workers are set by the wage determination of this topic.
